topic_info.title: Neuromyelitis spectrum disorders (transverse myelitis and neuromyelitis optica)

list.listitem: Suspect transverse myelitis (TM) in patients with progressive weakness and spinal cord dysfunction. Neuromyelitis optica typically presents with unilateral ocular pain and loss of visual acuity. Together they make up neuromyelitis spectrum disorders (NMSD).C
If clinically suspected, order MRI of C-, T- and L-spine, lumbar puncture with CSF analysis, and AQP4-IgG (aquaphorin antibody) blood test. C
Chronic therapy to prevent relapses include eculizumab, inebilizumab, rituximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and low dose corticosteroids (see . B
Treat underlying cause if possible, in conjuction with appropriate specialists. C

background.definition: Neuromyelitis spectrum disorders (NMSD) consist of related conditions characterized by inflammation most commonly of the optic nerve and spinal cord. Transverse myelitis (TM) is a non-traumatic, focal acute demyleination of the spinal cord only, without brain or optic nerve involvementl. Neuromyelitis optica is a related condition consisting of TM accompanied by severe optic neuritis.

list.listitem: In US and Europe, NMSD makes up about 1% to 2% of CNS inflammatory demyelinating disease. Prevalence higher for non-white populations including Black and Asian.
In patients with post-poliomyelitis disease, between 1 in 125 and 1 in 800.
Post vaccination: 1/212,500 per year following Hep B vaccine, 0.4/1,000,000 after HPV vaccine, overall 0.8/1,000,000 per year in children in the US state of California.
Among children immunized with OPV, 2 to 4/1,000,000 children; none with IPV.
In sub-Saharan Africa, 1% to 5% of TM cases are attributed to spinal schistosomias.
Up to 10% of patients with TM are eventually diagnosed with multiple sclerosis.
Immune mediated inflammatory spinal cord or optic nerve injury, either as part of a disease process or idiopathic.

Disease processes include autoimmune disorders, malignancies, infections (e.g. Epstein Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, Dengue, SARS-CoV-2) and CNS disease, especially multiple sclerosis.Drug use has been implicated in some cases.
Neuromyelitis spectrum disorders associated with Aquaporin 4 IgG antibodies is an immune astrocytopathy.
TM involves blood brain barrier breakdown and inflammation within a focal area of the spinal cord.

In patient with idiopathic TM, up to 40% have had an infection within 1 month, although no infectious agents can be recovered at the time of TM and most patient have recovered from the illness (73% resp, 13% GI, 13% flu like). This apparently triggers the astrocytopathy.
Suspect transverse myelitis (TM) in patients with progressive weakness. Suspect neuromyelitis optica in patients with ocular pain and loss of vision, especially if unilateral. C
If clinically suspected, order MRI of the spine, perform CSF analysis. C
The AQP4-IgG (aquaphorin antibody) blood test is highly specific and moderately sensitive for NMSD.C

Differential.Differential_Features: Brain MRI findings, optic neuritis may be present, oligoclonal bands in CSF
Trauma history, structural abnormality or compression on MRI
Ascending paralysis, usually lack of bladder dysfunction

list.listitem: The most common presenting symptoms for transverse myelitis are back pain and leg weakness, but TM can affect any location in the spinal cord. At maximum symptoms, approximately 50% of patients have lost all leg movement, most have bladder dysfunction, and 80 to 94% experience numbness, paresthesias, or band-like dysesthesias.
Patients with neuromyelitis optica typically present with unilateral ocular pain and loss of visual acuity, although it can be bilateral.

Signs of myelopathy may include bilateral sensory, motor, or autonomic dysfunction, including upper- and/or lower-motor neuron weakness, normal or decreased reflexes, a clearly defined sensory level (most often numbness), bowel and/or bladder dysfunction, and erectile dysfunction.
Involvement of the area postrema can cause protracted hiccups, nausea, or vomiting.
Review history for systemic diseases (autoimmune, malignancy, infectious and CNS diseases), and travel history. Prior therapuetic radiation suggests post radiation injury, not acute TM.
Fever may or may not be present for idiopathic TM.

Symptoms of idiopathic TM typically peak between 4 hours and 21 days, with complete emergence, but not necessarily resolution, of symptoms within 60 days. Symptoms peaking in less than 4 hours suggest spinal cord ischemia.
Visual disturbances suggest optic nerve involvement.
Younger age and being female are suggestive of TM.

Evaluate for spinal cord compression via neuroimaging, preferably T2 weighted MRI. MRI may demonstrate demyelination of the spinal cord without external compression. Assess for closed head trauma or peripheral nerve trauma.

Evaluate for other neurologic diseases including MS, HTLV-1-associated myelopathy/tropical spastic paraparesis (HAM/TSP), current infections (including viral, bacterial, and parasitic causes, as well as hematologic malignancies, autoimmune diseases, and sarcoidosis) through appropriate neuroimaging and laboratory analysis, including CSF. This may include MRI of the brain to evaluate for MS. MS like Brain MRI abnormalities have a high risk of conversion to MS.
Aquaphorin 4 specific autoantibodies, also known as NMO IgG, are recommended for all patients with clinically suspected NMSD. In one study they were 80% sensitive and 100% specific.
For patients with clinically suspected NMSD, but negative aquaphorin antibodies, obtain antibodies to myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG).

Idiopathic TM: absence of other CNS diseases active infection, connective tissue disease, or hematologic malignancy. The CSF should exhibit pleocytosis (>5 WBC/mm3 in children >2 months of age; >15 WBC/mm3 in children <2 months of age), >10 WBC/mm3 in adults with a negative gram stain and culture; CSF IgG level may be elevated.
EMG can help differentiate between transverse myelitis and Guillian-Barre.
Somatosensory response studies (SSERs) should be abnormal in transverse myelitis.
Signs and symptoms include bilateral sensory, motor, or autonomic dysfunction attributable to the spinal cord, with a clearly defined sensory level.
Perform complete neurologic exam, obtain MRI of the spine, rule out spinal cord compression, perform CSF analysis, obtain aquaorin 4 specific autoantibodies, and consider referral to a neurologist.
Evaluate for other neurologic diseases (multiple sclerosis, current infection, hematologic malignancy, autoimmune diseases, neurolmyelitis optica).
Provide appropriate supportive care for symptoms. C
Treat the underlying disease if possible. C
For acute attacks, IV corticosteroids are the standard of care, although there is no clinical trial evidence. Plasma exchange may be offered if steroids do not help. C
Chronic therapy to prevent relapses include eculizumab, inebilizumab, rituximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and low dose corticosteroids (see . B

Although there have not been any randomized trials, IV steroids (methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily for 5 days) is first line treatment for acute attacks of NMSD. Plasma exchange may be offered to those failing IV steroids.
Medications to prevent relapse are summarized in

A clinical trial randomized 230 patients in a 3:1 ratio to 300 mg IV inebilizumab or placebo on days 1 and 15. The study was terminated early because of a clear reduction in the likelihood of an attack in the treatment group (12% vs 39%, p < 0.001, NNT = 4).
Another monoclonal antibody, eculizumab, also reduced the likelihood of an attack in AQP4-IgG positive patients (3% vs 43%, p < 0.001, NNT = 2.5).
In an RCT with 83 patients with neuromyelitis optica, satralizumab (targetting IL-6) reduced the likelihood of relapse over 2 years (20% vs 43%, HR 0.38, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.88).

All patients with AQP4-IgG seropositive disease should take medfications for relapse prevention, as well as those with AQP4-IgG negative disease and a demonstrated history of relapses. For chronic prevention of relapse in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders, options include eculizumab, rituximab, azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil and low dose corticosteroids. These differ considerably by cost and side effects.

Two commonly recommended options are 1) azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil, with 6 months of corticosteroid therapy as a bridge until azathioprine or mycophenolate mofetil are fully active then tapered, 2) or immunotherapy with rituximab or eculizumab.
A network meta-analysis comparing it to mycophenolate mofetil and azathioprine found that rituximab was more effective.
Selective dorsal rhizotomy, a neurosurgical procedure may offer benefit in selected patients with continued spasticity.
Physical and occupational therapy as indicated.
Provide appropriate supportive care for all patients.
Treat underlying disease state including infection, CNS disease, malignancy, and autoimmune disease. See EE chapters on specific disease treatment.
Patients with suspected TM should be referred to a neurologist.
Consider referral to a rheumatologist or infectious disease specialist if clinically indicated.
Hospitalize patients with severe symptoms causing acute disability for monitoring and subsequent rehabilitation.
A relapsing course is most common, with months to years between attacks.

A study of 441 patients with 1976 relapsing attacks found the following were predictors of relapse: female, younger age at onset, and multiple sclerosis disease modifying drugs. Use of immunosuppresants was associated with less relapse. Patients with optic neuritis at onset were more likely to become blind.
Approximately one third recover with little to no sequelae, one third are left with moderate degree of permanent disability, and one third have severe disabilities. B
Multiple sclerosis may initially present with TM and up to 79% in one series progressed to MS.
The most common long term consequence of TM is bladder dysfunction.
Most patients with idiopathic TM recover quickly (days to weeks), but recovery may be incomplete.
